definition: In machine learning and pattern recognition, a feature is an individual measurable property or characteristic of a data set.
details: Choosing informative, discriminating, and independent features is crucial to producing effective algorithms for pattern recognition, classification, and regression tasks. Features are usually numeric, but other types such as strings and graphs are used in syntactic pattern recognition, after some pre-processing step such as one-hot encoding. The concept of "features" is related to that of explanatory variables used in statistical techniques such as linear regression.

explainer.lead: A feature is one measurable property of the data, such as a person's height or the length of an email. The features you choose shape what a pattern-recognition, classification, or regression algorithm can learn, so picking useful ones is a central part of building an effective system.

tiers.eli5: Imagine sorting fruit by looking at its colour, size, and weight. Each of those clues is a feature: one thing you can measure about a fruit. A learning program uses clues like these to tell things apart or make predictions, and good clues make its job much easier.
tiers.practitioner: Features are the measurable inputs used for classification, regression, and other pattern-recognition tasks; choose them for being informative, discriminating, and as independent as possible. They are usually numeric, while strings and graphs can be used in syntactic pattern recognition after pre-processing, with one-hot encoding as one example. Adding more properties is not automatically better if they do not help the task.
tiers.paperLevel: For an observation x, a feature is an individual measurable property or characteristic phi_j(x), and a collection of such features provides the representation consumed by a classification or regression algorithm. The concept is related to explanatory variables in statistical methods such as linear regression. Feature quality matters: informative, discriminating, and independent features are crucial to effective algorithms.

explainer.example: To classify emails, one observation could be represented by two features: its length in characters and whether a chosen word appears. If an email has 420 characters and contains that word, its feature values are 420 and 1; another email with 85 characters and without the word has values 85 and 0, giving the classifier measurable differences to work with.

usedIn.name: Pattern recognition
usedIn.detail: Features supply the measurable characteristics used to recognize patterns in data.

usedIn.name: Classification
usedIn.detail: Informative and discriminating features help algorithms distinguish between categories.

usedIn.name: Regression
usedIn.detail: Features act as measurable inputs for predicting numeric outcomes and relate to explanatory variables in linear regression.

explainer.intuition: A feature is one clue about an observation, not the observation as a whole. A good set of clues captures differences that matter for the task without relying on redundant or unhelpful measurements.
howItWorks: Identify measurable properties of each observation in the data set.
Select properties that are informative and discriminating for the task, favouring independence between features.
Represent the features numerically where needed, using pre-processing such as one-hot encoding for suitable non-numeric values.
Pass the resulting representation to a pattern-recognition, classification, or regression algorithm.
explainer.whyItMatters: Algorithms work with the properties they are given, so weak or redundant features can limit classification and regression performance. Choosing informative, discriminating, and independent features is therefore crucial to producing effective algorithms.
misconceptions: A feature is not an entire data set or observation; it is one measurable property or characteristic.
Features are usually numeric, but strings and graphs can also be used after appropriate pre-processing.
More features do not automatically mean a better algorithm; their usefulness, discrimination, and independence matter.
